title: Week1
content:
AWS Free Tier and Cost Management Week 1: 28 September–4 October 2026.
Results updated: 9 October 2026.
The first week focused on creating an AWS account, using the Console, completing the five credit activities, and setting up cost management before deploying workloads. This report combines the practice notes with the latest confirmation of completion.
Program lessons and labs studied Week 1 covered two lessons in Section 1 — Explore AWS Services of the First Cloud Journey roadmap. Each program section contains multiple lessons and labs and may span several weeks.
Lesson/lab ID Content studied Practice results 000001 — Create an AWS Account / AWS Free Tier 2025 Account creation, Free Plan and Paid Plan, AWS Credits, basic services introduced through five activities, Monitoring & Cost Optimization, and FAQ. Created an account, completed five credit activities, received $200 credits, and upgraded to Paid Plan. Individual monitoring outcomes are documented below. 000007 — Manage AWS costs with AWS Budgets AWS Budgets concepts and the distinction between cost and usage budgets. Configured Cost Budget and Usage Budget. Scope of completion: The five credit activities belong to lesson 000001. Basic EC2, Bedrock, Lambda, and RDS practice in this lesson does not establish completion of their separate in-depth labs or all of Section 1. RI Budget and Savings Plans Budget have not been recorded as implemented.
Week 1 objectives Understand Free Plan, Paid Plan, and AWS Credits tracking. Complete five activities and understand the basic roles of EC2, Amazon Bedrock, AWS Budgets, AWS Lambda, and Amazon RDS. Set up Cost Budget, Usage Budget, and Project Spend Limit. Explore Cost Explorer, resource checks, and measures to limit unexpected charges. Weekly content allocation The table organizes learning content across working days from the internship start date of 28 September 2026. It is a content allocation, not a verified daily record of when each action took place. The report update on 9 October falls in Week 2.
Day Date Learning and practice Reference Monday 28/09/2026 Learn about AWS Free Tier; create an account; explore the Console, Free Plan, and Paid Plan. AWS Free Tier 2025 Tuesday 29/09/2026 Complete the EC2 and Amazon Bedrock activities; learn about virtual servers and AI foundation models. Five credit activities Wednesday 30/09/2026 Complete the AWS Budgets activity; create Cost Budget and Usage Budget; explore alert thresholds. AWS Budget workshop Thursday 01/10/2026 Complete the Lambda and RDS activities; learn about serverless computing and managed relational databases. Five credit activities Friday 02/10/2026 Review all five activities; check credits, Paid Plan, and spend limit; set up Cost Explorer and study Monitoring & Cost Optimization and FAQ. AWS Free Tier 2025 Dates in tables use DD/MM/YYYY.
Overall results Figures recorded at the check documented in the report updated on 9 October 2026:
Item Result AWS Account Created; Console in use Credit activities 5/5 completed, as confirmed in the latest practice update Available AWS Credits $200.00 Account plan Upgraded to Paid Plan Recorded charges / amount due $0.00 / $0.00 Project Happy Path — Within limit Project Spend Limit $20/month Cost Budget Configured Usage Budget Configured Cost Explorer Initial setup complete; awaiting data Five activities and learning outcomes The activity list follows the AWS Study Group guide. Completion reflects my latest practice confirmation.
Activity Status Basic knowledge gained Launch an EC2 instance Completed Virtual servers; roles of AMIs, instance types, and security groups. Use Amazon Bedrock Playground Completed AI foundation models; submitting prompts and viewing responses. Set up AWS Budgets Completed Budget monitoring and cost alerts. Create a web app with AWS Lambda Completed Running functions with serverless computing. Create an Amazon RDS database Completed AWS-managed relational databases. The earlier unresponsive Aurora/RDS create button was an obstacle during a previous attempt. The RDS activity is now recorded as completed based on the latest confirmation; the cause of the earlier issue remains undetermined.
AWS Budgets and Cost Explorer Configured Cost Budget to monitor spending and Usage Budget to monitor service consumption. Their tracking goals and units differ, as explained in the AWS Budget workshop.
The Budgets screenshot shows daily-budget-10 ($10), monthly-budget-25 ($25), and monthly-budget-50 ($50), all with OK status and $0.00 used. It illustrates the budget list; it does not show the detailed Usage Budget configuration or successful delivery of alert emails.
Happy Path has a separate $20/month Project Spend Limit. The Budgets interface states that budgets do not set hard spend limits; creating a budget does not imply that every resource will stop automatically.
Accessed Cost Explorer and completed initial setup. Explored Unblended Cost, daily tracking, service grouping, and identifying Top 5 Cost Drivers. At the check, AWS was preparing data and requested another check after 24 hours; there was no data available to identify the highest-cost services.
Resource monitoring and outstanding items Item Practice result Emergency Cost Control Checked Billing Dashboard and EC2 in the inspected Region. No EC2 instances were found; recorded charges were $0 with $200 credits remaining. No emergency shutdown was needed. CloudWatch Billing Alerts Not implemented: no AWS/Billing metrics were visible, and Billing Preferences displayed an Enterprise AWS requirement at the check. Recorded as an observed limitation; the final cause has not been verified. Resource tagging through Tag Editor Not implemented: AccessDeniedException with an explicit deny in an AWS Organizations SCP. AWS CloudShell Unavailable at the check due to an account verification in progress message. Custom CloudWatch Metrics Studied; the Lambda function for publishing cost metrics has not been implemented. This is separate from the Lambda credit activity. Studied resource auditing and stopping non-critical EC2 instances when needed. Checking one Region does not establish resource status across all Regions.
Practice screenshots Figure 1 — Console shows $200 credits and $0.00 monthly charges before the plan upgrade. The screenshot does not display the five activity statuses; the 5/5 result is based on the practice confirmation.
Figure 2 — Created budgets and the $20 Happy Path Project Spend Limit.
Figure 3 — Billing shows $200 available credits, $0 amount due, and Happy Path within its $20 limit. The Paid Plan upgrade is recorded from the practice confirmation; this Billing screenshot does not display the account plan name.
Lessons learned Understand the five services better through practice and monitor costs before deploying further workloads. Studied credit eligibility, charges that may not be covered, and the one-time reward for each activity through the FAQ. Distinguish configuration errors from IAM/SCP restrictions, account verification, and data preparation delays. Record completed activities, setup awaiting data, and unimplemented features separately. A $0 balance at one check does not guarantee that future charges will remain zero. Summary: Completed the Week 1 foundations: created an AWS account, completed five activities, received $200 credits, upgraded to Paid Plan, and configured Cost Budget, Usage Budget, and Project Spend Limit. Outstanding advanced monitoring items are documented separately for follow-up.

title: Event 1
content:
Event Report: Buildrathon Kickoff — Code the Future with CMC Global Event: Buildrathon Kickoff: Code the Future with CMC Global — FCAJ Buildrathon 2026 (Season 01)
Date and time: Saturday, September 26, 2026, 09:00 – 12:00
Location: AWS Vietnam office, 26th floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City
Role: Attendee
Organizers: AWS Study Group / First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ), in collaboration with CMC Global.
Event Objectives The event launched FCAJ Buildrathon 2026 (Season 01), bringing members of the Cloud and AI community together to build practical products on AWS. It introduced the Buildrathon journey, shared experience with deploying AI agents in enterprises, and provided opportunities to connect with experts from FCAJ and CMC Global.
For me, it was an opportunity to explore how cloud computing and AI can address a specific problem and to prepare my approach to learning and teamwork for the internship.
Speakers Thien Lu — Program Manager, First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ). Phong Pham — Program Manager, First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ). Bui Nhat Truong (Truong Bui) — Technical Leader, CMC Global; speaker for “The Thinking Behind Building The Bot”. Event Agenda Time Session 09:00 – 09:30 Buildrathon kickoff and program introduction 09:30 – 11:15 Talkshow: “The Thinking Behind Building The Bot” 11:15 – 12:00 Mock-interview with CMC Global Key Highlights Building Practical Products through Buildrathon The program introduced a six-month Buildrathon journey focused on applying Cloud and AI knowledge to products with practical value. My takeaway was that a product needs to be evaluated for its ability to solve a problem, its stability, and its potential to develop beyond the demo stage.
This helped me connect learning individual AWS services with designing a complete system. A team should start with user needs and requirements before deciding how to organize data, processing, and deployment.
“The Thinking Behind Building The Bot”: Designing AI Agents Bui Nhat Truong’s session explored how to structure an AI agent system. It helped me understand the roles of three components:
Planning: breaking a request into steps that serve the intended goal. Memory: maintaining context within a session and managing information needed across sessions. Tools: connecting to APIs, data sources, or functions to perform tasks using actual data. Enterprise agents also need to connect with knowledge sources and internal services. Data flows, access boundaries, and control over agent actions therefore need attention from the beginning of the design process.
Preparing AI Systems for Operation The session discussed balancing accuracy, response time, and cost when selecting models and designing processing flows.
I also noted several concerns to address before deployment:
Checking responses to reduce unsupported information or answers inconsistent with the input data. Handling failed tool calls and outputs that do not follow the expected format. Logging and tracking processing steps to investigate errors. Testing both common scenarios and edge cases before expanding usage. Career Connections with CMC Global The final mock-interview session offered attendees an opportunity to explore career expectations and preparation for technical interviews. It reminded me to practice explaining my approach to a problem and the reasoning behind technical choices alongside developing technical knowledge.
What I Learned The event helped me understand how architecture, data, tools, and testing work together in an AI application. When designing an agent, I need to consider where its data comes from, which actions it can perform, and how each step’s result can be verified.
I also recognized that AWS knowledge becomes more meaningful when connected to a specific problem. Studying Cloud, data, and AI within a complete processing flow helps me understand the contribution of each component.
For teamwork, the kickoff highlighted the value of exchanging ideas, sharing knowledge, and agreeing on goals. These are habits I want to maintain while learning with the FCAJ community.
How I Plan to Apply These Lessons Clarify the problem before implementation: identify users, input data, expected outcomes, and evaluation criteria. Connect AWS learning with practice: explore how storage, processing, and access controls work together in an application. Experiment with agents incrementally: start with a small scope and check tool use and error handling before expanding. Practice technical communication: explain architectures, solution choices, and areas for improvement. Learn actively with the team: discuss problems and record lessons to share with other members. My Experience Attending the kickoff at the AWS Vietnam office with other members of the group gave me more motivation for my Cloud and AI learning journey. The discussions about enterprise AI agents helped me understand the expectations involved in building a practical product.
Meeting people and connecting at the event was also memorable. The session gave me direction to learn with clear goals, exchange ideas proactively, and gradually turn knowledge into products.
Proof of attendance Xóm Data’s LinkedIn post about the Kickoff, with my name in the list of participating teams: View the LinkedIn post. Event Photos Figure 1: Event poster introducing the speakers, schedule, and venue.
Figure 2: Group check-in at the “It’s Still Day 1” lobby beside the “The Thinking Behind Building The Bot” standee.
Figure 3: Group photo with the speakers in the conference room.

content:
IAM, policies and AWS CLI practice Week 2 period: 05/10/2026–11/10/2026. Report updated: 11/10/2026.
Learning scope: Section 1 — Explore AWS Services; Region/AZ review, user/group/role sections of 000002, AWS CLI lab 000011, and application role concepts/configuration related to 000048. CloudShell 000049 is on hold due to an error.
This week focused on distinguishing identities from permissions, practicing IAM in the Happy Path account, and simulating narrowly scoped policies. IAM objects were created, an AdminRole session was used, and the learner confirmed completion of 000011. Screenshots support profiles, EC2 reads, S3, IAM, SSH and SNS email delivery; application role 000048 still awaits EC2-to-S3 verification.
Week 2 objectives Objective Completion criteria Distinguish Region/AZ and AWS identities. Explain Region/AZ, AWS account, Builder ID, root, IAM user and role sessions; identify unverified security settings. Practice users/groups and Switch Role. Create IAM objects, sign in and confirm an active AdminRole session; record cleanup status. Read policies and apply least privilege. Explain Effect/Action/Resource/Condition; simulate Allow, implicit deny and explicit deny. Understand application roles. Distinguish trust/permissions policies, explain temporary credentials and configure a narrowly scoped EC2 S3 read role. Continue CLI and live permission testing. Check profiles/Region and read/manage resources; separately verify the caller and a before/after test of one narrow permission. Tasks for the week The table is a content allocation based on all seven week 2 notes, not confirmation that tasks took place on the scheduled dates. Actual dates have not been recorded; the update date is not substituted for practice dates.

Completed creation/role switching scope; cleanup reported in practice notes. 000002 — IAM Tuesday — 06/10/2026 Read policies and least privilege; simulate S3 permissions and SecureTransport. Completed simulation scope according to learner confirmation. IAM Policy Simulator Wednesday — 07/10/2026 Study application roles; configure EC2 trust and S3 photos read permissions. Completed according to learner confirmation and screenshots. 000011 — Installation Friday — 09/10/2026 EC2 reads, S3 and SNS. Completed; EC2 output, S3 cleanup and SNS email available. Learning and lab details Region/AZ and the lab account A Region is a geographic area with multiple AZs; each AZ contains one or more Data Centers. Separate infrastructure supports fault isolation. Applications must be designed and deployed appropriately to benefit from multiple AZs; selecting a Region does not deploy across every AZ.
The lab account is Happy Path. The Builder ID configuration session uses AccountFullAccessRole; IAM users and root are separate identities. Following Advanced features activation, the account is managed through AWS Organizations and the Console displays multiple Regions. The IAM Identity Center team name differs from AdminGroup. Learned that activation cannot be reversed and removes existing spend limits; budget alerts are not automatic spending caps. AWS documentation
MC-06 indicates MFA/passkey for AdminUser, while OperatorUser shows — at capture time. Builder ID/root MFA, a separate strong root password and root access keys remain unverified; IAM user MFA does not establish root security.
To be added — Account security: Builder ID/root MFA for Happy Path, root credential and access key status, and inspection dates. Region/resource/AZ observations in the notes are insufficient to complete the inventory.
000002 — IAM users/groups and Switch Role References: Create group/user, Create role/user, Switch Role, Cleanup.
Created AdminGroup and AdminUser; reported using AdministratorAccess and adding the user to the group. MC-03 shows the group before any members; MC-04 shows one group membership without its name or policy details. Created AdminRole and OperatorUser, signed in as OperatorUser and switched roles. MC-05 confirms role creation; MC-06 confirms the AdminRole session can read the users list. Learned that roles are not attached to users/groups as permissions policies. A switched session uses role permissions instead of the original user permissions; switching back does not undo changes. No separate test after switching back is available. Reported deleting AdminUser, OperatorUser, AdminGroup and AdminRole; this does not imply cleanup of all account resources or system roles. To be added — Cleanup evidence: Post-cleanup Users, User groups and Roles screenshots/logs confirming the four lab objects are absent, with inspection dates.
Policies and least privilege — supplementary simulations for 000002 Studied Effect (Allow/Deny), Action (API), Resource (ARN scope), Condition, and granting only necessary permissions. The example policy allows only s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::fcaj-example-bucket/photos/*.
The following results are recorded from the learner’s confirmation of completing Tuesday’s guided practice; individual simulation screenshots/output have not been checked:

Allow with Condition aws:SecureTransport = true; context true / false Allowed / implicit deny within the tested policy. Objects refer to the example bucket; its existence is not claimed. The Simulator does not make live S3 API calls. An unmet condition prevents that Allow from applying; it is not an explicit HTTP deny across the bucket. Simulator documentation
To be added — Policy evidence: Allow, implicit deny, explicit deny and SecureTransport screenshots/output, tested policies/context and inspection dates.
000048 — Application role: theory and configuration Distinguished trust policies (who can assume the role) from permissions policies (what the role can do). Studied the flow: EC2 associated with an instance profile containing the role → application obtains temporary credentials through instance metadata → SDK signs requests → S3 evaluates permissions. Applications do not use Console passwords; avoid embedding long-term access keys in code. AWS guide
According to Wednesday’s note and learner confirmation, configured fcaj-ec2-photo-reader, trusting ec2.amazonaws.com with sts:AssumeRole, and inline policy ReadPhotosOnly allowing s3:GetObject under photos/* in the example bucket. No screenshots are available to check actual names/configuration.

000011 — Introduction to AWS CLI Program section: Section 1 — Explore AWS Services. Reference: BTC lab 000011.
Knowledge: Credentials authenticate requests; policies determine permissions. A profile does not grant permissions. Distinguished profile/Region/output/query, bucket/object, topic/subscription, IAM user/group and SSH connections.
Environment: Windows PowerShell, Happy Path account. Screenshots show access keys from the shared credentials file, not aws login. title: Event 2
content:
Event Report: AWS Cloud & AI Day Hanoi — Watch Party: Ho Chi Minh City Event: AWS Cloud & AI Day Hanoi - Watch Party: Ho Chi Minh City
Date and time: Tuesday, September 29, 2026; badge collection from 08:00, keynote starting at 09:00 (Vietnam time, UTC+7).
Location: Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City; registration and badge collection on the 26th floor, as stated in the confirmation email.
Attendance format: Watching the Hanoi program online with other members at the Ho Chi Minh City viewing location.
Role: Attendee
Organizer: AWS Vietnam, with support from sponsors and technology partners.
Event Objectives AWS Cloud & AI Day 2026 offered an opportunity to learn how enterprises use Cloud and AI to address practical software development, infrastructure, data, and operational needs. The technical and business discussions explored building systems that can operate reliably, scale, and remain manageable in terms of cost.
My aim was to connect the AWS concepts I am learning with practical architectures and understand the requirements involved in bringing AI applications into enterprise use.
Speakers and Participating Organizations The program featured AWS experts alongside representatives from enterprises, partners, and educational institutions. Organizations associated with the key technical topics included VPBank, Cloud Kinetics, G-AsiaPacific Vietnam, NTQ Solution, Samsung R&D Center, GEM, SoftwareOne, VinUni, and VIB, alongside a security expert’s session.
Their topics covered Platform Engineering, application modernization, security, AI agents, infrastructure automation, and cost governance.
Event Agenda Schedule for September 29, 2026, in Vietnam time (UTC+7).
Time Activity 08:00 Registration and badge collection on the 26th floor of Bitexco, followed by seating 09:00 Watch the keynote online 10:15 Break and networking 11:00 Watch the morning technical sessions 12:05 Lunch and networking 13:10 Watch the afternoon technical sessions 14:50 Break and networking 15:20 Watch further technical sessions 17:00 End of the program I attended the Watch Party at Bitexco in Ho Chi Minh City and watched the Hanoi program online. The following sections summarize notable topics from the event for my report.
Key Highlights Platform Engineering and Application Modernization on Amazon EKS VPBank — Platform Engineering at Scale: explored building Internal Developer Platforms on Amazon EKS to support engineering workflows. This helped me understand how a shared platform can standardize deployment practices and reduce repetitive work. NTQ Solution — Legacy Migration to EKS: discussed migrating NestJS applications from EC2/PM2 to EKS with GitOps. My takeaway was that modernization involves deployment processes, configuration management, and subsequent operations as well as infrastructure changes. Choosing Appropriate Architectures and Managing Storage Costs Cloud Kinetics — Don’t use a Ferrari to Get Phở: emphasized choosing architectures suited to the problem and sizing resources according to actual needs. It encouraged me to consider suitability, cost, and operational effort when comparing solutions. GEM & SoftwareOne — Stop Overpaying for Storage: addressed Amazon S3 Storage Classes and cost-effective data lifecycle management. I learned to consider access frequency and retention requirements before choosing a storage approach. Workload Identity and Security The Beyond IAM Roles topic introduced a broader perspective on workload identity and zero-trust security design. It highlighted the need to consider each component’s identity, the resources it can access, and how interactions between components are controlled.
I want to explore this further while practicing IAM and deploying AWS applications, particularly systems with multiple services or agents that use tools.
AI in Software Development and Infrastructure Automation G-AsiaPacific Vietnam — AI-DLC: explored integrating AI into the software development lifecycle as a teammate. I noted the importance of using AI within a defined process, checking its output, and keeping responsibility for results clear. Samsung R&D Center — Multi-Agents for IaC: discussed using multiple AI agents for infrastructure deployment and automated IaC drift remediation. This introduced me to the problem of deployed configurations diverging from their declared state and the potential role of AI in detecting and addressing those differences. Agent Orchestration and AI Cost Governance VinUni — Agent Harness & Frameworks: covered multi-agent orchestration with Strands, LangGraph, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It gave me direction for exploring how processing flows, tools, and agent collaboration can be organized around complex requests. VIB — Bedrock Cost Control: addressed near real-time AI spending controls and financial governance at enterprise scale. It showed why budget monitoring and usage limits need consideration during application design. What I Learned My main takeaway was the shift toward platforms that can operate over the long term. Cloud and AI applications need to be considered alongside observability, security, cost controls, and incident handling.
The EKS and GitOps examples helped me understand why enterprises standardize deployment workflows. Architecture choices still need to match the problem’s scale and the team’s capabilities. I want to practice explaining why a service is appropriate for a requirement.
For AI systems, quality depends on data, tool orchestration, review processes, and operational limits. AI innovation needs engineering discipline to produce reliable products.
How I Plan to Apply These Lessons Start architecture decisions with requirements: establish the problem and expected scale before selecting AWS services. Explore EKS and GitOps: build on container fundamentals, deployment workflows, and configuration management. Practice S3 data management: classify data by access frequency, retention needs, and cost. Strengthen IAM knowledge: pay attention to least privilege and workload identities. Review AI-assisted work: check generated code, configurations, and explanations before using them. Include cost in design criteria: track resource usage and estimate budgets from the experimental stage. My Experience Although the main event took place in Hanoi, watching online with other members at the Bitexco Watch Party in Ho Chi Minh City gave me an opportunity to learn in a community setting. The event’s topics helped me connect my current cloud studies with concrete enterprise requirements.
Breakfast and conversations with other members were also memorable. The experience gave me more motivation to continue studying AWS and AI and gradually develop the thinking needed to build practical systems.
I appreciate AWS Vietnam and the supporting organizations for making enterprise Cloud and AI engineering experiences accessible to the community.
